Calcium oxalates: burning in the mouth, drooling, vomiting when leaves are chewed. Usually limited to irritation; an exam is warranted if the animal refuses food.
Calcium oxalates: burning and irritation of the mouth, drooling, vomiting. There is usually no systemic poisoning, but an animal with mouth pain and loss of appetite should be seen by a vet.
Saponins: nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea from eating the leaves. Toxicity is moderate; the main thing is not to let them chew on it regularly.
Anthraquinones and saponins in the leaf skin: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy; the gel inside the leaf is mildly toxic. Don't use aloe to "treat" your pet — the irritation outweighs any benefit.
caution.caution: Anthraquinone glycosides (aloin) in the latex layer

caution.description: Milky sap (ficin): irritation of skin and mucous membranes, drooling, vomiting; sensitive animals may develop dermatitis. Severe poisoning is rare.
Calcium oxalates in all parts of the plant: irritation of mucous membranes, drooling, vomiting. Severe poisoning is rare; keep it out of reach, and see a vet for persistent vomiting.
Saponins, concentrated mostly in the leaves: drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain with a large amount eaten. Contact with the sap can irritate the skin.
caution.caution: Triterpenoid saponins (hederagenin), leaves more toxic than berries

caution.description: Triterpenoid saponins, concentrated mostly in the tubers: severe vomiting, diarrhea, and, if a tuber is eaten, heart rhythm disturbances and seizures. If a dog digs up and eats a tuber, go to the clinic immediately.

Its "deadly" reputation is greatly exaggerated: the milky sap irritates the mouth and stomach — drooling, a single bout of vomiting. Serious poisoning is a rarity, but don't let pets chew on it regardless.
Geraniol and linalool: vomiting and reduced appetite in cats and dogs, dermatitis on contact. The toxicity level is moderate.
Saponins: vomiting (sometimes with blood), drooling, and in cats — dilated pupils and unsteadiness. It usually resolves on its own, but repeated vomiting and lethargy call for a vet visit.

Alstroemeria ("Peruvian lily") is NOT a true lily and is not lethal to cats: it is considered mildly toxic. The sap can irritate skin and mucous membranes, and eating it may cause mild GI upset. Don't confuse it with Lilium/Hemerocallis lilies, which are lethally toxic to cats.

Roses are not toxic. The danger is the thorns (mouth and paw injuries) and treatments used on cut flowers: bouquet roses may be sprayed with pesticides and preservatives — don't let pets drink the vase water.
Peonies contain paeonol — eating them causes vomiting and diarrhea, but serious poisoning is uncommon. Keep bouquets out of reach, especially from kittens and puppies that chew on everything.

Eucalyptus (branches in bouquets, the essential oil, and "eucalyptus shower" products) is toxic: eucalyptol causes drooling, vomiting, and weakness; the oil is especially dangerous for cats, which lack the enzyme to process it. An oil diffuser in a room with a cat is also a risk.

The "mimosa" from spring bouquets — silver wattle — is not toxic to cats or dogs. The pollen may irritate the airways of sensitive animals; it's still best not to let them chew the branches themselves — the fibers are coarse.

Soluble calcium oxalates, most concentrated in the tubers and roots. Dogs and cats get drooling and vomiting; kidney failure has been described in grazing animals that ate large amounts. Ate a tuber or a lot of leaves — see a vet.
The toxic principle is unknown. After eating it — vomiting, lethargy, sometimes a wobbly gait. If signs appear, see a vet.

Insoluble calcium oxalates (as in spathiphyllum and monstera): intense burning in the mouth, drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing. Systemic poisoning is usually absent, but with mouth pain and refusal to eat — see a vet.
Insoluble calcium oxalates: burning in the mouth, drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing. Systemic poisoning is usually absent, but with mouth pain and refusal to eat — see a vet.
Saponins: vomiting in dogs and cats. The stiff, sharp-edged leaves can injure the mouth. If vomiting repeats — see a vet.

unsafe.description: Theobromine is toxic: vomiting, arrhythmia, seizures. Dark chocolate is more dangerous than milk chocolate. If ingested — see a veterinarian immediately.
Destroys red blood cells causing hemolytic anemia. Dangerous in any form: raw, cooked, powdered, in prepared dishes and baby food.
unsafe.caution: Organosulfur compounds (n-propyl disulfide) — oxidative damage to red blood cells

unsafe.description: Persin is toxic to many animals; the pit adds an intestinal-obstruction risk. For birds and rabbits avocado is deadly even in small amounts.
unsafe.caution: Persin; the pit is also an obstruction hazard

unsafe.description: Toxic even in small doses: respiratory depression, coma. Never, in any form.
Caffeine is a cardiac toxin for animals: tachycardia, tremors, seizures.
Dough keeps rising in the stomach: bloat plus fermentation ethanol. Baked bread is a separate question — raw dough is dangerous.
unsafe.caution: Fermentation: gastric distension plus ethanol production

unsafe.description: Most adult animals stop producing lactase — result is diarrhea. Cow's milk is no substitute for mother's milk in kittens and puppies either.
unsafe.caution: Lactose intolerance in most adult animals

unsafe.description: A little low-fat unsalted cheese or cottage cheese is an acceptable treat; fatty and salty cheeses are not.
Macadamia nuts are toxic to dogs; other nuts mean fat, salt and obstruction risk. Cats do not need nuts at all.
unsafe.caution: Macadamia: unidentified toxin (weakness, hyperthermia in dogs); other nuts: fat, salt, obstruction risk

unsafe.description: Raw pork carries Aujeszky's disease and parasite risk. Feed meat cooked or after deep freezing.
unsafe.caution: Raw pork: Aujeszky's disease (pseudorabies) and parasites

unsafe.description: Sugar leads to obesity and diabetes; chocolate and xylitol in sweets are outright toxic. Pets should not get sweets.
Salted and smoked foods strain kidneys and heart; spices irritate the gut. Sausage is not pet food.
unsafe.caution: Sodium overload; spices and preservatives irritate the GI tract

unsafe.description: Rhubarb leaves have a high oxalate concentration: kidney damage. Give to no one.

Grayanotoxins: even a few leaves cause vomiting, weakness, bradycardia, and a drop in blood pressure; coma is possible. One of the genuinely dangerous houseplants/garden plants — if eaten, go straight to the clinic.
One of the most poisonous ornamental shrubs: cardiac glycosides, lethal to all species.

Contains bufadienolides — cardiac toxins: vomiting, diarrhea, and at high doses, heart rhythm disturbances. A folk "medicinal" plant, but dangerous for pets. If eaten, go to the clinic — don't just watch and wait.
Caustic milky sap: burns to mucous membranes, drooling, vomiting; if it gets in the eyes, keratitis can result. Keep all euphorbias out of pets' reach; if eaten, rinse the mouth and go to the vet.

Lycorine and other alkaloids, most concentrated in the bulb (as in daffodils): vomiting, drooling, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, lethargy, tremors. Ate a bulb or part of the plant — see a vet straight away.
